# Should I swap my gas boiler for a heat pump?

*Typical English 3-bed semi on the Ofgem price cap (Oct-Dec 2026). Prices and efficiency come from the sources at the bottom; everything else is a flagged assumption. Every figure below is generated by `heatpump_model.py`, so you can change an input and regenerate the file (see 'Re-run it').*

*Who this is for: an owner-occupier in England with a mains-gas boiler and a wet (radiator) system, deciding on money. It will mislead you if your home is off the gas grid, is a flat, is in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, or if carbon, comfort or future boiler rules matter more to you than cost. Figures are rounded: this is a forecast, not a quote.*

*In plain terms: **SCOP** is how many units of heat a heat pump delivers per unit of electricity (3.0 means 3). A **heat-pump tariff** is electricity priced lower at certain times of day. More terms are explained in the glossary near the end.*

## The answer

> **Verdict: NO on a standard tariff; TOO CLOSE on a heat-pump tariff**  
> **Confidence: High (on a standard tariff the simulation agrees with this in 94% of 5,000 draws)**

- **Bottom line:** don't do it just to save money on a standard tariff. On a heat-pump tariff it roughly breaks even, so it comes down to the efficiency your installer predicts and whether you value the non-financial benefits.
- **Over 15 years, a heat pump on a standard tariff leaves you £4,100 worse off than keeping a gas boiler** (£4,800 worse off in today's money). On a heat-pump tariff you'd be £1,150 worse off (£2,550 worse off in today's money).
- **As an investment:** over 15 years the extra money you put into the heat pump loses about 10% a year on a standard tariff and loses about 2% a year on a heat-pump tariff. Compare that with what the same money would earn in savings or by paying down debt.
- **Running costs barely differ; the up-front cost is what decides it.** In year 1 the heat pump's bills are £35 lower on a standard tariff or £190 lower on a heat-pump tariff, but you pay £7,500 after the grant. Keeping the boiler means paying £2,500 for a new one in year 5, which narrows the gap but doesn't close it.
- **Why bills are so similar:** a kWh of heat costs about 9.4p from your gas boiler and 9.2p from a heat pump at SCOP 3.0 on the standard tariff. Electricity (with VAT) costs 3.5x as much per kWh as gas, which cancels out most of the heat pump's efficiency.

### What would flip it

| If... | Today's assumption | The heat pump breaks even over the period when... |
|---|---|---|
| Your installer's **predicted SCOP** (efficiency) is higher | 3.0 | 4.16 or more on a standard tariff, 3.33 or more on a heat-pump tariff |
| You get a **cheaper electricity tariff** for heating | 27.6p standard; 22.1p assumed heat-pump tariff | 19.9p/kWh blended or lower, at SCOP 3.0 |
| The **installed price** is lower | £7,500 | £2,550 or less (standard tariff), £6,100 or less (heat-pump tariff) |
| Your home uses more **gas** | 10,500 kWh/yr | no realistic level (standard tariff), 14,664 kWh/yr or more (heat-pump tariff) |
| Your **boiler is failing soon** | replaced in year 5 | see the 'when the boiler would need replacing' row in the drivers table |

The simulation below says the three things that move the result most are: heat pump efficiency, fuel price paths, and heat-pump tariff price. Of all the inputs, efficiency and tariff price can be pinned down before you buy; future fuel prices can't.

Rule of thumb: ask installers for a written heat-loss calculation and a predicted SCOP. If it is below the SCOP in the first row, the heat pump is unlikely to pay back on running costs alone.

## The 15-year picture

Total cash spent from today (heat pump installed now vs. keeping the boiler and replacing it in year 5). Prices rise each year as set in the assumptions. A positive 'heat pump ahead by' means the heat pump has cost less in total.

| Year | Keep boiler: total spent | Heat pump (standard tariff): total spent | Heat pump ahead by | Heat pump (heat-pump tariff): total spent | Heat pump ahead by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | £0 | £7,500 | -£7,500 | £7,500 | -£7,500 |
| 1 | £1,050 | £8,500 | -£7,450 | £8,350 | -£7,300 |
| 2 | £2,100 | £9,550 | -£7,450 | £9,200 | -£7,100 |
| 3 | £3,200 | £10,600 | -£7,400 | £10,100 | -£6,900 |
| 5 | £8,000 | £12,800 | -£4,800 | £12,000 | -£3,950 |
| 7 | £10,400 | £15,150 | -£4,750 | £13,950 | -£3,550 |
| 10 | £14,150 | £18,850 | -£4,700 | £17,050 | -£2,900 |
| 12 | £16,850 | £21,500 | -£4,650 | £19,250 | -£2,400 |
| 15 | £20,400 | £24,500 | -£4,100 | £21,550 | -£1,150 |

The heat pump starts £7,500 behind and claws it back through lower bills. Neither tariff breaks even within 15 years. The step in the 'keep boiler' column at year 5 is the replacement boiler. Remaining life of each system at the end is credited at what you paid, spread evenly over its lifespan (a notional value, not a sale price).

## How well does the answer hold up?

**Simulation.** I varied every uncertain input at once (5,000 random draws around your inputs: efficiency, gas use, installed price, boiler age and cost, fuel price rises, tariff price, whether VAT returns). The ranges are my judgement, centred on the base case and spelled out in `monte_carlo()`; they are not measured spreads.

| | Heat pump cheaper in... | Typical result (median) | 80% of draws fall between | More than £2,000 worse off | More than £2,000 better off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard tariff | 6% of draws | -£3,500 | -£6,500 to -£650 | 75% | 1% |
| Heat-pump tariff | 44% of draws | -£330 | -£3,150 to +£2,600 | 22% | 16% |

**What matters most.** Each row moves one input between plausible extremes and shows the heat pump's advantage at each end (positive = heat pump ahead after the full period). Rows are ranked by how far they move the result.

| Input (extremes tested) | Standard tariff | Heat-pump tariff |
|---|---|---|
| Heat pump efficiency (SCOP 2.6 to 4.0) | -£6,400 to -£440 | -£3,000 to +£1,750 |
| Fuel price paths (elec dearer: gas +2%/elec +4% to elec cheaper: gas +4%/elec +2%) | -£6,550 to -£1,700 | -£3,350 to +£1,050 |
| Heat-pump tariff price (no load shifting to mostly shifted; heat-pump tariff only) | -£4,100 to -£4,100 | -£2,650 to +£1,500 |
| Net installed price (£9,000 to £5,500) | -£5,350 to -£2,450 | -£2,400 to +£500 |
| When the boiler would need replacing (never in period to now) | -£5,400 to -£3,400 | -£2,450 to -£480 |
| Home's gas use (8,000 to 13,000 kWh/yr) | -£4,100 to -£4,150 | -£1,850 to -£470 |
| Keep gas connected (yes to no) | -£5,450 to -£4,100 | -£2,500 to -£1,150 |
| Replacement boiler cost (£2,000 to £3,500) | -£4,450 to -£3,450 | -£1,500 to -£500 |
| VAT on electricity (5% returns, to holiday made permanent) | -£4,100 to -£3,350 | -£1,150 to -£550 |
| Existing boiler efficiency (90% to 78%) | -£4,350 to -£3,750 | -£1,250 to -£1,050 |

**Self-test.** The model must reproduce numbers it didn't make up:

- Pass: Ofgem typical bill reproduced within £1 (£1,724 vs £1,723)
- Pass: Nesta running-cost parity (ratio 3.3, efficiency 2.8, boiler 85%; Nesta rounds, so within 1%) (boiler £1,050 vs heat pump £1,052)
- Pass: Hand-derived flat-price case (model +£1,000 vs by hand +£1,000)
- Pass: Higher efficiency never hurts

## Using this with an installer quote

Ask each installer for: (1) a room-by-room heat-loss calculation, (2) the predicted SCOP at your design flow temperature, (3) the total price with the grant already deducted, and (4) whether radiators or a hot-water cylinder need replacing and are included. ## When to re-check

- **By 25 November 2026:** Ofgem confirms the January-March cap (reported date). Re-run with the new unit prices.
- **31 March 2027:** the electricity VAT holiday ends under current rules (Ofgem). The model already assumes it does; if it is extended, set `elec_vat=0`.
- **When your boiler is on its last legs:** set `boiler_replace_year=0`; that is the case most favourable to the heat pump.
- **When you have an installer quote:** use the grid above, then re-run with their SCOP and price.
- **If you are on a fixed-price deal:** your prices differ from the cap; enter your own unit rates.

## What I checked against evidence

Each main assumption was tested against source material. Items marked **Changed** replaced my starting estimate in all the figures above.

| Starting assumption | What the evidence says | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Electricity price stays at the published 26.32p | [Ofgem](https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/news/changes-energy-price-cap-between-1-october-and-31-december-2026): that rate excludes VAT, and VAT is removed only until 31 March 2027. With VAT it is 27.64p, so the electricity-to-gas price ratio is 3.47, not 3.30. | **Changed.** Treating a six-month tax holiday as permanent would flatter the heat pump for 15 years, so the base adds 5% VAT back. The holiday made permanent is shown as a row in the drivers table. |
| A typical home uses 9,500 kWh of gas | The government's [NEED dataset](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-energy-efficiency-data-framework-need-report-summary-of-analysis-2026/national-energy-efficiency-data-framework-need-report-summary-of-analysis-2026-accessible-webpage) puts the 2024 median for all homes in England and Wales at 10,000 kWh and the mean at 11,200 kWh. It gives no figure for semi-detached homes in its text. | **Changed** to 10,500 kWh (my estimate for a 3-bed semi, between the median and mean). Ofgem's 9,500 is a pricing convention and is still used for the bill check. |
| Replacement boiler costs £3,000 | Published 2026 guides give £2,000-£3,500, with a median combi swap about £2,300 (commercial sources). | **Changed** to £2,500. |
| Heat pump net price £7,500 (your figure) | A secondary source citing Boiler Upgrade Scheme data gives a median installed price about £13,000 before the grant, so about £5,500 net. At £5,500 net the heat-pump-tariff result would be +£500. | Kept your £7,500; get quotes, because the price is one of the larger drivers. |
| The grant is £7,500 and has no strings about gas | [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/heat-pump-grants-increased-by-50-per-cent): £7,500 for an air-source heat pump, scheme extended to 2028, no requirement to disconnect gas. | Confirmed. Keeping gas connected is an option and is shown as a driver. |
| A heat-pump tariff costs 20p | Octopus's published Cosy structure gives the relative prices (table below); it doesn't give current unit rates. | **Changed** from a flat 20p to 80% of the standard rate, so it follows the price you actually pay. |
| Heat pump efficiency (SCOP) 3.0 | The Electrification of Heat median is 2.8 (interim). I could not get household-level data to test the spread. | **Not tested against raw data.** It is the largest driver in the table above, so get the installer's predicted SCOP. |
| Fuel prices rise in step | Cornwall Insight forecasts a January 2027 cap of about £1,999 (reported), but I found no electricity/gas split. | **Not tested.** It is the second-largest driver in the table above. |
| Gas can be disconnected cheaply | I found no source for the disconnection cost. | **Not tested.** The model assumes it is free. |

**What a heat-pump tariff really costs depends on when you use power.** Octopus Cosy's cheap rate is 49% of the day rate and its peak is 150%, with cheap windows 4-7am, 1-4pm and 10pm-midnight and peak 4-7pm:

| How the heat pump is run | Price as a share of the standard rate | Pence per kWh now |
|---|---|---|
| Left on all day with no shifting | 87% | 24.1p |
| Avoids 4-7pm, otherwise evenly spread | 78% | 21.6p |
| Avoids 4-7pm, 40% in cheap windows (assumed in the model) | 80% | 22.0p |
| Heavily shifted: 70% in cheap windows | 64% | 17.8p |

**Sources and how far to trust them**

- Price cap: [Ofgem unit rates and standing charges](https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/node/176588/), average Direct Debit, Oct-Dec 2026 (electricity 26.32p/kWh + 54.83p/day; gas 7.97p/kWh + 29.68p/day). Official. Note the electricity rate excludes VAT, which is removed only until 31 March 2027; the model adds 5% back. These are averages across England, Scotland and Wales, not England-only, and the price cap changes every quarter.
- Typical use (9,500 kWh gas, 2,500 kWh electricity): Ofgem's 2026 review, as reported by [Energy UK](https://www.energy-uk.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Energy-UK-Explains-Typical-Domestic-Consumption-Values.pdf). I could not open Ofgem's own decision page, but these figures with the cap prices reproduce Ofgem's £1,723 typical bill to within £1 (see the check in the script output).
- Heat pump efficiency: [Electrification of Heat trial](https://es.catapult.org.uk/news/heat-pumps-shown-to-be-three-times-more-efficient-than-gas-boilers/) (Energy Systems Catapult), median seasonal efficiency 2.8 for air-source heat pumps. These are interim results from the 742-home trial; I did not find the final report. [Nesta](https://www.nesta.org.uk/report/how-to-make-heat-pumps-more-affordable/assumptions-and-methods/) assumes a baseline of 3 rising to 3.3. [Carbon Brief](https://www.carbonbrief.org/factcheck-what-it-really-costs-to-heat-a-home-in-the-uk-with-a-heat-pump) reports that the Heat Pump Monitor site shows about 3.9; the article doesn't say how those systems were recruited and the figure is defended by the site's co-founder, so I treated 3.9 as an upper case, not the typical one.
- Grant: [GOV.UK, Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/heat-pump-grants-increased-by-50-per-cent): up to £7,500 for an air-source heat pump in England and Wales. The GOV.UK page says the scheme was extended to 2028; an installer blog says it was overhauled in April 2026 and runs longer, which I could not confirm. Check GOV.UK for the current end date. The £7,500 net cost is your figure.
- Heat-pump tariff: [Octopus Cosy](https://octopus.energy/smart/cosy-octopus/) publishes its structure (cheap rate 51% below the day rate, peak 50% above it, peak window 4-7pm) and [average rates](https://octopus.energy/press/Octopus-Energy-launches-new-off-peak-rate-for-heat-pump-customers/) (about 13p / 26p / 40p). The page doesn't state current unit rates, so I use only the ratios and assume the day rate is close to the standard rate. Check live rates for your region before relying on it.
- Running-cost parity check: [Nesta](https://www.nesta.org.uk/feature/energy-affordability/establish-price-ratio-target/) states that at a price ratio of 3.3 a heat pump with efficiency 2.8 costs the same to run as an 85%-efficient gas boiler; the self-test reproduces that.
- Not sourced at all: boiler and heat pump lifetimes, replacement boiler cost, service costs, future price rises.

## Plain-English glossary

- **SCOP / seasonal efficiency:** units of heat delivered per unit of electricity over a year. 3.0 means 1 kWh of electricity gives 3 kWh of heat. A gas boiler delivers about 0.85-0.9 kWh of heat per kWh of gas.
- **kWh:** the unit your meter and bills use for energy.
- **Standing charge:** a fixed daily fee for being connected. If you disconnect gas completely you stop paying the gas one, which is worth roughly £108 a year; the electricity one stays.
- **Price cap:** Ofgem's limit on the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can charge on standard tariffs. It is not a limit on your total bill.
- **Boiler Upgrade Scheme:** a government grant that comes off the installer's price.
- **Heat-pump tariff:** electricity that is cheap at certain times of day. It only helps if your heat pump and hot-water heating can run mostly in the cheap windows.
- **Simulation / draws:** the model is run 5,000 times, each time with every uncertain input nudged to a different plausible value (a 'draw'). The share of runs where the heat pump wins is a guide to how safe the verdict is.
- **Median:** the middle result when all the runs are lined up from worst to best.
- **Hot-water cylinder:** the insulated tank a heat pump needs to store hot water, replacing the combi boiler's instant hot water. It is usually part of the installed price.
- **SPF vs SCOP:** SPF is efficiency measured in a real home over a year; SCOP is the predicted figure for a design. Both mean units of heat per unit of electricity.
- **MCS / heat-loss calculation:** MCS is the certification scheme installers need for the grant. A heat-loss calculation is the room-by-room estimate of how much heat your house loses, which sizes the heat pump and predicts its SCOP.
- **Today's money:** future savings reduced slightly because £100 later is worth less than £100 now.

## Limits

- This is a model with typical inputs, not a survey of your house. A proper heat-loss calculation from an installer will replace my efficiency assumption.
- Not counted: higher home value, carbon savings, any radiator or pipework upgrades beyond the net price you gave, installation disruption, extra running cost of a hot-water cylinder, solar panels, and what happens if the grant ends.
- Electricity standing charge is the same in both cases, so it's left out.

## Re-run it

```
python3 heatpump_model.py --list                          # see every input
python3 heatpump_model.py --set gas_kwh=12000 --set scop=3.4   # try your own numbers
python3 heatpump_model.py --set gas_kwh=12000 --write heat-pump-vs-gas-boiler.md   # regenerate this file
python3 heatpump_model.py --check heat-pump-vs-gas-boiler.md   # confirm the file matches the model
```
